blocks.text: The third of those eight birds is the סוגא (Chulin 62b). The word סיג means fence, and from it סוגה enclosure; it is possible, then, that סוגא is the wren [German Zaunkönig, "fence-king"]. The bird is so called because it flutters singing from fence to fence (Beumer: Populäre Naturg. p. 236).
The Brambling.

The fourth of those eight birds is the הרנוגא (Chulin 62b). The word may be compounded of הר "mountain" and נוגא (in the sense of נגה, to dwell). However, we must admit that the notion of dwelling on, or among, mountains is very elastic, and would be equally applicable to the mountain falcon, the mountain pheasant, the mountain magpie, the mountain thrush, etc.; but the brambling [German Bergfink, "mountain finch"] belongs to the sparrow genus, from which, as we have seen, some species have already been named (§. 213 and 214).
The Black Woodpecker.

The fifth of those eight birds is the כוחילנא (Chulin 62b), which Landau derives from כחל "black colour" and translates as black woodpecker. But who would wish to determine this explanation, here too, as the only correct one? There is a blackbird, a black tit, a black duck, etc., and so נקבל היא קבלה אם
—; it is only a pity that Landau gives his explanation a priori and merely at random.
The Coot.
The sixth of those eight birds is the בר נפחא (Chulin 62b) "son of blowing", perhaps the coot [German Blashuhn, "blowing hen"] (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 381). Landau wavers between coot and plover.
On בר see above p. 2, note *.
The Moorhen.

The seventh of those eight birds is the מרדא (Chulin 62b), which is also called תרנגולא דאגמא "cock of the reeds". Our passage states: At first there was doubt about the מרדא with regard to its purity; later Rabbi Papa said that the bird תרנגולא דאגמא is forbidden, whereas the bird תרנגולתא דאגמא "hen of the reeds" is permitted to be eaten; still later it was seen that the latter bird, too, presses its food firmly to the ground and tears pieces from it in the manner of birds of prey (§. 23), whereupon the eating of the תרנגולתא דאגמא, which is identical with the name גירוחא, was also forbidden.

The Tosephot (ibid.) rightly remark that no distinction is made here between cock and hen of one and the same species, since it is inconceivable that at first the male of the moorhen was forbidden and the female permitted; rather, two distinct species are meant here, of which the one was called תרנגולא דאגמא "reed cock" and the other תרנגולתא דאגמא "reed hen".
Most probably the different species of the moorhen are meant here; for there is a larger species and several smaller species (Voigt l. c.
[p. 180] 2. p. 380), of which the larger was presumably called הרנגולא "cock" and the smaller הרנגולתא "hen";

but perhaps the following distinction may have been made here: the הרנגולא דאגמא, which was also called מררא "refractory", "wild", may be the wild bittern, which is untameable and fights even against the strongest dogs and is stubborn; it was regarded from the outset as forbidden, because it (Ardea stellaris) belongs to the heron genus (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 362); it is much larger than the moorhen and was therefore called הרנגולא "cock"; the moorhen, on the other hand, the smaller and easily tamed bird, was perhaps called גירוחא for that reason, from גור "to dwell", "to abide", with reference to its capacity for staying in human habitation.

Difficult to determine is the following statement made by the Talmud. As an equivalent for the forbidden bird גירוחא, the tongue of the כורא (fish) is permitted to be eaten (Chulin 109b). Which fish is meant here is not said; the Tosephot (M. Katan 11a) also believe that a particular fish is to be assumed, but do not specify it further. I therefore venture to express a conjecture, although it admittedly does not agree with the view of Rashi. He takes גירוחא in the latter Talmud passage and the same bird name at Chulin 62b as the name of one and the same bird, namely that of the moorhen, and the taste of this bird is said to be like the taste of the fish tongue. But why should the tongue of the fish in particular have a taste distinct from the rest of the fish's flesh? And which fish could this be? I, however, take the גירוחא mentioned in Chulin 109b to be the name of the woodpecker. This bird has a horny tongue set with pointed, backward-directed spiny bristles, just like the tongue of the fish. I therefore derive גירוחא from גרר, whence מגרה "saw", since the tongue of the woodpecker is set with spines like a saw. I need hardly say that this conjecture is highly daring, and I only remark further that Jalkut Schimoni (Ps. fol. 130, col. 3), which enumerates several similar equivalents, leaves precisely גירוחא and כורא unmentioned; the same is the case in Midr. R. Wajikra fol. 191, col. 1.
The Steppe Lark.

The last of those eight birds, finally, is the הושלמי (Chulin 62b), of which it is said that it is very lustful and mounts many foreign birds (Sanhedrin 108a). Read also הלשמי, and this spelling might serve for the following identification. הל means "heap of rubble", and שמי "wasteland, steppe", and I would conjecture the steppe lark here. The reason for the doubt concerning the purity of the said eight birds was discussed above (§. 212). In these birds the membranes of the stomach are difficult to separate from one another, and in fact the lark has a muscular stomach, so that it can digest small stones in the manner of fowl (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 215). The muscular part is, as is well known, the inner hard membrane of the stomach, and in the lark it may be difficult to detach from the outer membrane.
More decisive is that statement about lustfulness, for the lark belongs to the sparrow genus, whose lustful nature is well known.
